#1985. Werder Bremen vs Hamburger SV - prediction, team news, lineups

By Anthony Nolan | 20 Nov 2026 23:59, Last updated: 21 Nov 2026 04:57

Werder Bremen will be battling to keep their unlikely European dream alive on Sunday, when they welcome Hamburger SV to the Weserstadion for a Bundesliga Nordderby.

Die Werderaner are hoping to bounce back from defeat last time out, while HSV are keen to pick up where they left off prior to the international break.

Daniel Thioune guided Werder to safety last term after taking the helm in early February, though his sights are set much higher this time around with his team sat in a strong position upon the league's return.

Nine matches into the campaign, Die Werderaner are sixth in the Bundesliga table, where their tally of 15 points has them two clear of seventh-placed Elversberg and just three shy of RB Leipzig in fourth.

Securing European football of any variety would be a major accomplishment for Thioune, who is currently in his first top-flight role as manager, not to mention that the club last appeared on the continental stage back in the 2010-11 Champions League group stage.

However, Werder signed off for the international break with a 1-0 defeat at Stuttgart on November 7, their second loss in three matches after a 3-2 beating by Borussia Dortmund in the DFB-Pokal in late October.

In fairness to the Green-Whites, they fought back from 2-0 down against BVB thanks to a brace from Niclas Fullkrug, only to lose out to a stoppage-time free kick by Marcel Sabitzer.

Additionally, a 2-0 victory over Hoffenheim between those defeats saw the hosts maintain their unbeaten streak on home turf this season, where they will hope to record a fourth win in five outings on Sunday.

Meanwhile, Merlin Polzin's Hamburger endured a dire start to the season, conceding 12 goals without reply in their first three Bundesliga games before firing back with a run of three consecutive triumphs.

It would be fair to say that HSV's term has been defined by streaks so far, alternating between trios of defeats and wins across all competitions, and the club will be hoping to stabilise after the international break.

Polzin's side were held to a 1-1 draw by Croatia's Hajduk Split in a friendly on November 15, following up a 3-1 success against Borussia Monchengladbach that helped to distance the team from the relegation zone in the German top flight.

That victory has left Hamburger 11th in the Bundesliga table with 12 points to their name - a total that puts them level with Eintracht Frankfurt, Hoffenheim and Stuttgart up to eighth - as well as five points clear of 16th-placed Union Berlin.

Earning another win on Sunday would be keeping with HSV's pattern this term, but after seeing the visitors lose four of their five away league matches in 2026-27, fans would be forgiven for harbouring doubts.

Werder will be without strikers Keke Topp (ACL) and Salim Musah (thigh) once again as they recover from long-term injuries, though the doubts about Marco Grull's fitness after he missed training with a calf issue will be a major concern for the team.

If Grull is sidelined on Sunday, then expect to see Niclas Fullkrug supported up top by Eren Dinkci, Chuki and Justin Njinmah.

Jens Stage and Skelly Alvero are also unavailable due to respective thigh and calf injuries, while question marks remain about the readiness of fellow midfielder Senne Lynen, who has been ill over the past week, though Youri Regeer and Ludovit Reis should be on hand to form Thioune's double pivot.

Elsewhere, the versatile Mitchell Weiser is a doubt with a thigh problem and left-back Moussa N'Diaye is recovering from a groin injury, so Arthur and Olivier Deman look set to start at full-back.

As for Hamburger, they are missing centre-back Jordan Torunarigha, who has been dealing with a hip issue, but Mario Vuskovic is likely to return after getting over a minor back injury.

The visitors are lighter in midfield than ideal, with all three of Albert Sambi Lokonga (calf), Bilal Nadir (thigh) and Nicolai Remberg (ACL) sidelined, so Martin Adeline could join Miro Muheim in the centre of the park, while Albert Gronbaek operates in the number 10 role.

Centre-forward Yussuf Poulsen is also out with a calf injury, but Terem Moffi and Patson Daka will be ready to lead the line in a strike partnership on Sunday.

Hein; Arthur, Friedl, Pieper, Deman; Regeer, Reis; Dinkci, Chuki, Njinmah; Fullkrug

Heuer; Capaldo, Omari, Bornauw; El Ouahdi, Adeline, Muheim, Moller Wolfe; Gronbaek; Moffi, Daka

Werder have been exceptional on home turf this season, and they will be expecting to collect all three points once again, but the match is likely to be closer than otherwise if Grull remains sidelined.

By contrast, Hamburger have struggled on the road throughout 2026-27, and with four defeats in five away Bundesliga games so far, expect to see the visitors' overall pattern of results broken.

#1984. Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli not feeling the heat after dismal Nations League campaign

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:30 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 17:40 EST, 17 November 2026

Sebastien Pocognoli insists he’s unconcerned about calls for his head after a dismal start to his time in charge of Scotland.

Monday’s 4-0 defeat to Switzerland confirmed that the Belgian’s side finished a distant third in their Nations League section with the only two wins in six games coming against North Macedonia.

After a decent start to the match in St Gallen, Scotland fell behind to a Lewis Ferguson own goal and the result was put beyond doubt when the Swiss scored two quick goals at the outset of the second half.

With another performance falling way short of expectations and little sign of progress, the new manager is increasingly coming under pressure.

Despite only being in charge for 13 weeks, pundits including Michael Stewart have already called on the Scottish Football Association to draw a line under Pocognoli’s reign.

Adamant that he’s not feeling the heat, though, the 39-year-old insisted: ‘I am not thinking about this. I am just looking ahead to the next camp in March and the start of the qualification.

Scotland head coach Sebastien Pocognoli is confident he'll get Scotland back on track

Skipper Andy Robertson reacts at full-time to the 4-0 defeat against Switzerland

‘We have to take the most we can from the last two camps and try to build something strong for the next one. The objective is to reach the Euros in the best position possible.

‘We will have ups and downs and it was not good in terms of the score against Switzerland. But, for me as a coach, it was a good game to see us against a strong nation away from home. That’s something we have to take into the future.’

Asked how he dealt with the growing clamour for his dismissal, he replied: ‘I don’t accept this to be honest. It’s always like this when you have a bad moment, when you think about the past. But always thinking about the past is an energy taker — we have to look forward.’

The successor to Steve Clarke, Pocognoli has tried to bring in a more attacking philosophy via a 3-4-2-1 formation.

While his reluctance to adapt has also drawn widespread criticism, he claims he’s not averse to coming up with a different approach.

‘It’s possible,’ he added. ‘I did it in Monaco and we won many tough games with a back four. I also won many good games with a back three.

‘We played in the Champions League and in half of the games we played with a different shape, so it doesn’t mean that I’m not flexible. But the timeline is to do what we are trying to do now.’

Asked if the job was proving to be tougher than he anticipated, Pocognoli said: ‘No. I think we nearly had a good game. It was just the score and the aspects in the boxes. That’s where there’s disappointment.

‘It’s step by step. And we have created a lot of chances in four of the six games. And in these six games we played one of them with 10 men and another where we were not on the level at all against Slovenia.’

#1981. Leny Yoro wrongly sent off, Fernandes rages: Three Sam Barrott howlers in Liverpool vs Man United

Senior Correspondent AUTHORITY Senior football correspondent and podcast host with specialist knowledge across the Premier League and SPFL. FOCUS Transfer news, breaking stories, and behind-the-scenes insight across Arsenal, Liverpool, Celtic, and Manchester United. THE INSIGHT Callum utilises a network of club and industry contacts across the Premier League and SPFL to deliver verified, high-speed reporting. He provides the depth behind the headlines — from breaking transfer news to behind-the-scenes developments — ensuring fans get the full story as it happens.

Sam Barrott was a busy man in the middle of the park as he oversaw Liverpool's win against Manchester United.

The 34-year-old took charge of the fiery derby clash at Anfield in what proved to be a difficult day for the officials live on Sky Sports.

Barrott was immediately given a big call to make as Leny Yoro was sent off after just eight minutes after crashing into Alexander Isak when he was through on goal.

The resulting free kick was slammed home by Dominik Szoboszlai, and just three minutes later, Florian Wirtz volleyed the ball in to give Andoni Iraola's side a 2-0 lead.

Goals from Rio Ngumoha and Victor Munoz made it 4-0 in the second half as Liverpool eased away from their rivals, sparking further concerns about the Red Devils' form.

Barrott, however, could find himself at the centre of many of the discussions and while the referee was far from the one to blame, some fans are not happy.

As previously mentioned, the biggest flashpoint in the game came after just eight minutes, as Yoro was shown a straight red card for bringing down Isak on the edge of the box.

While it seemed a relatively straightforward decision at the time, replays quickly showed it was more subjective, as it may not have been a clear opportunity.

The striker's touch was well out of his feet, and questions have been asked about whether he would have met it ahead of the on-rushing Senne Lammens.

To illustrate how difficult the decision was, former PGMOL chief Keith Hackett first told Football Insider that the decision was clear, before reviewing footage which later made him dub the call "subjective".

Yoro's red card was not the only decision which left the Man United fans, players and coaches frustrated, as Bruno Fernandes confronted the referee later in the game.

In the 57th minute, the Portugal international raced after a ball which split the Liverpool defence, only to collide with the covering Jeremy Jacquet.

A free kick was given in favour of the Liverpool defender, launching Fernandes into an explosion of frustration towards the referee after he felt he was hard-done-by.

The attacking midfielder insisted the contact was shoulder-to-shoulder, while also suggesting he had his shirt pulled, but his explosive cries fell on deaf ears.

In the end, Fernandes was probably fortunate to avoid a yellow card for his outburst.

Another decision which went against Man United at Anfield came earlier in the first half, although with Pochettino's side 2-0 down at the time, it would not have changed much.

In the 25th minute, a ball was fizzed into the feet of Matheus Cunha in midfield, as as he attempted to take it on the turn, Alexis Mac Allister slid through the back of him.

Despite winning the ball, the Argentina midfielder's trailing leg caught the back foot of Cunha, leaving him in a heap, but Barrott was not moved to brandish his card.

It was another of multiple decisions which went against the Red Devils, and while they cannot be used as excuses, they will feel harshly treated by the match officials.

#1979. De Winter discusses importance at Milan, Amorim’s position and the future: “One of us”

Koni De Winter spoke at an event at the AC Milan store today, and he covered numerous topics with a lot of openness.

This season, De Winter has found himself in a new, important light. Matteo Gabbia spent most of pre-season in the middle of the back three, but injuries have prevented him from playing much of a role in the campaign.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

It’s an unfortunate shame and there may have been some worries about De Winter taking on this role. However, he’s taken the opportunity in his stride, looking every part a starter in Ruben Amorim’s defence.

Rumours about a new defender arriving will persist, so it’ll be interesting to see what happens with his minutes from January onwards. However, he’s created something of a headache, but it’s a good one to have.

Speaking to SportMediaset on the sidelines of the Meet&Greet at the Milan Store in San Babila, via MilanNews, De Winter looked at the rise in his playing time, Amorim’s closeness to the group and much more.

You also took over at Reggio Emilia when Gabbia was unfortunately injured. You’re practically always there; what does that mean to you?

“I’m playing a lot, it’s great to be playing. We’re playing a lot, and these days you train more on taking care of your body, keeping healthy, and right now I’m doing that more, but it’s great to be playing a lot of games. Playing a lot of games for Milan, and it’s even better to win games.”

It’s all great, but it wasn’t a given: you’ve earned this place as leader. Do you now feel like a leader of this AC Milan?

“I feel good at this Milan club, and as I always say, I try to give what I can. It’s also true that I might have a more important position this year. That might be true, but I always try to do my part, give my all, and help my teammates.”

It’s clear, evident, that Amorim holds you in high regard, but what is Amorim like? An adjective.

“I’d say he’s very human. He’s one of us, he laughs, he has fun, but when he has to be serious, he’s serious. He lives with the group, the group feels close to him, and I think that gives the players a good feeling. It’s nice to work for him and with him.”

Is it true that he got very angry after the defeat against Ferencvaros?

“Yes, but I think the whole group felt that we had played a very poor game, so, as I saw it, my teammates saw it too.”

Are Ferencvaros and Bologna two games you’re ready to say “never again” to? Will Frosinone be a different team?

“Yes, exactly, as I said, we are very confident, but sometimes even too much so, and then all matches are difficult against whoever we play against, and we have to understand this quickly and we can’t make the same mistakes.”

Among the various critics, it’s said that this AC Milan team has enormous potential, but there are too many ups and downs. Does it need more consistency?

“Yes, I think it hurts even more when we lose because we know we can do well, we can win every game. So yes, when we really lose, in the locker room you feel like we’ve let ourselves down first and then everyone else.”

You recently became the father of a beautiful baby girl. What are your nights like as a dad?

“At night, I’m fine. My girlfriend is working really hard, so it’s a lot for me. I mean, I get up sometimes, but it’s much quieter. I think it’s harder for her.”

And how much has life changed with the arrival of a daughter?

“It’s changed a lot, I mean, I don’t know how to explain it. When you’re at work, you think about your daughter, you want to come home earlier, you want to hold her, you want her – I mean, you have more beautiful moments – but it’s hard to explain. I don’t know how to explain it.”

You were also used as a full-back, but now you only play as a centre-back…

“Good, good, because I also consider myself a centre-back, but it’s true that I can also play full-back. It’s something I can do, but it’s not my favourite position. But yes, it’s true that I’ve played a few games there in the past, but I’m happy playing as a centre back and I’m happy that the coach sees that too.”

“I mean, crazy in a good way, yes. He likes to have fun, he likes to dance, he likes to talk, so he’s a bright spot, as they say, for the locker room, yes.”

“Well, that’s a good question. Yes, I miss her. I thought about it even when the little girl was born: I also want to score a goal, I mean, dedicate a goal to her, so I miss her, yes.”

How do you concentrate when you’re in the hotel retreat? How do you focus in the hours leading up to kick-off?

“It’s become a routine now, so I always do the same things. You’re in the hotel, you take a shower, you play a little video game or you’re on your phone, so now I don’t even think about it, it’s really become a routine.”

“He says to stay focused on the game because, as we know, one moment can change the game and at Milan it can also change a season, so it’s very important not to underestimate every moment and always stay focused.

It seems to me that there is a great understanding between you and Strahinja Pavlovic even off the pitch…

“Yes, it’s true, he and I have a good relationship; we met last year. Then when you see him you might not think, I mean, I didn’t think he would be such a great friend, but we got along really well both on and off the pitch, it’s really nice to spend time with him.”

Our 007s at Milanello tell us about some great ping pong matches between you and Pavlovic. Who’s the better player?

“This is difficult, but he started at a much higher level than me. But now I’ve improved a lot, although I have to say he’s even stronger. But yes, every day we start with a game of ping pong and then we start working.”

Would you like your daughter to play soccer in the future? Are you planning a second child? Would you like to have a son who plays soccer?

“I want her to do what she wants, where she feels good, where she doesn’t feel pressured, and where she can express herself best. And then, going back to ping pong, I think there’s some video; maybe we can see me beat her.”

#1978. Mauricio Pochettino will never succeed at Man United, it is sad but painfully obvious

Senior Correspondent AUTHORITY Senior football correspondent and podcast host with specialist knowledge across the Premier League and SPFL. FOCUS Transfer news, breaking stories, and behind-the-scenes insight across Arsenal, Liverpool, Celtic, and Manchester United. THE INSIGHT Callum utilises a network of club and industry contacts across the Premier League and SPFL to deliver verified, high-speed reporting. He provides the depth behind the headlines — from breaking transfer news to behind-the-scenes developments — ensuring fans get the full story as it happens.

Mauricio Pochettino will never succeed as the Manchester United manager while he is forced to deal with the board's rotten decisions.

It is sad but painfully obvious to those watching United be torn apart by Liverpool in a defeat that felt so inevitable as soon as the manager's self-defeating teamsheet was announced.

Chief executive Omar Berrada claimed recently that the back line was not a concern for the board, while insisting the team are improving and heading in the right direction.

Just over one week later, Man United have been dispatched 4-0 against their biggest rivals in a pitiful display which could have ended in an even wider scoreline.

They now have, statistically, the worst defence in Europe's top five leagues, with 34 goals conceded across all competitions so far this season.

While none of that can be placed on Pochettino's shoulders after just three training sessions, they are the same issues which have seen three previous managers sacked.

Erik ten Hag, Ruben Amorim, and most recently Michael Carrick, have all met the same fate under this board and they are showing no signs of changing any time soon.

Former Man United assistant manager Mick Brown told Football Insider on 16 November, shortly following Pochettino's appointment, that he is destined to fail at Old Trafford.

Rather than being an indictment on the manager, though, the concerns are with the board and the chief decision-makers who will be key to any success United have.

If Berrada and his head of recruitment Jason Wilcox genuinely believe that this squad is good enough to compete, and that they've made the right calls, they must be ousted.

The CEO speaking about the depth of options in defence, after they were forced to play two 20-year-olds in the closing stages against Aston Villa, was bizarre to begin with.

After a 4-0 defeat to Liverpool, there can be no more excuses for the board, and they have got to change their stance or risk being left behind.

Pochettino has been thrown into a nightmare situation, regardless of the allure the club still has, and will now be given an impossible job to turn their situation around.

Unfortunately, should Man United continue to struggle, the blame will fall at his feet regardless of whether he is truly at fault, while any improvements will be in spite of the board.

It is not just the fans who have been left raging at the board and the decisions made in recent weeks, as key players have also felt compelled to speak out against them.

Lisandro Martinez was the first and most vocal of them, as he directly tore into Wilcox and Berrada, questioning their transfers and suggesting they had thrown Carrick under the bus.

Football Insider revealed last month that Man United are fearing a dressing room mutiny, with large sections of the dressing room unhappy with how things are going.

Carrick ultimately paid the price for that, but after players spoke out on social media following his departure, it is clear he is not the problem as far as they are concerned.

Martinez's comments, while misjudged in the moment, echoed the feelings of the majority of Man United supporters, and Pochettino will now face the same issues.

#1976. Keith Wyness reveals if Bundesliga club can tempt Everton into accepting Thierno Barry offer

RB Leipzig do not have the necessary financial power to tempt Everton into selling striker Thierno Barry any time soon.

That is according to former Toffees chief executive Keith Wyness, speaking exclusively to Football Insider, who believes that his former club have nothing to worry about when it comes to the Bundesliga interest.

Leipzig previously made contact over a move for Barry in the summer, and are showing a renewed interest after he has scored six goals in his opening 10 Premier League games this season.

However, Wyness does not believe that the Red Bull-backed side are capable of "threatening" Everton with a lucrative offer.

Barry has become a hugely important part of David Moyes' project this term, and he remains the only senior striker on Everton's books right now.

Wyness believes that the 24-year-old still has plenty to prove in English football, and does not expect him to depart Merseyside any time soon.

Everton’s former chief Wyness – who served as CEO at Goodison Park between 2004 and 2009 and now runs a football consultancy advising elite clubs – believes that Leipzig is the only potential move that Barry's agent may "promote" in the coming months.

However, he does not expect a switch to Germany to be something that the Frenchman gives any consideration to at all.

Speaking on the latest edition of Football Insider's Inside Track podcast, Wyness explained Everton's stance on Barry's future.

"The club that I've heard have been looking, or at least his agent would be trying to promote, is Leipzig. I don't think they're going to threaten Everton in terms of the sort of money they're going to be able to offer," he said.

"Look, to me he's still not proven. Yes, he's got some goals. They haven't been classic striker's goals, as many know. A few have been coming in off different parts of the body.

"But listen, they're goals, and we all appreciate it, and those goals have been a big part of Everton's good start to the season.

"But yet to me he's not proven himself as a prolific striker, and it's going to take another at least until Easter, and if he's consistent and he keeps on going until Easter then we're talking about a better valuation for a player."

Former Manchester United chief scout Mick Brown told Football Insider recently that Everton could yet accept a "huge" offer for Harrison Armstrong in January.

The Toffees blocked a £40million move to Nottingham Forest in the summer, but may yet take the chance to cash in and reinvest the profit into their squad.

Brown believes that Armstrong is one of few sellable assets in Moyes' squad, and also feels that they have ample cover for him in the midfield if he were to depart.

However, the homegrown ace is hugely popular among the fanbase, and it would take an eye-watering offer to tempt Everton to sell.

#1973. Pedro Neto is sent off for two yellow cards in under two minutes before bizarre touchline clash with Craig Bellamy - as Portugal beat Wales with Bruno Fernandes on target

Published: 17:34 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 17:49 EST, 17 November 2026

Chelsea star Pedro Neto lost his cool while playing for Portugal in their win over Wales as he received two yellow cards in as many minutes before clashing with opposing manager Craig Bellamy.

The Blues winger had in fact scored in the game, netting his side's second goal at the Cardiff City Stadium, but saw his game fall apart in the second-half.

He was first booked for a high challenge on the back of Brennan Johnson's leg – a tackle which some may argue could have been a red in itself.

One minute and 59 seconds later, he was shown his second yellow when he slid in on Johnson again. He didn't appear to make too much contact, if any, but left the Wales man sprawling to avoid it.

German referee Sven Jablonski showed no hesitation in sending Neto off, but the winger wasn't going to take it lying down.

He had to be held back by captain Bruno Fernandes as he tried to confront Johnson, and seemingly managed to shout in his direction before reluctantly making his way off the field.

Pedro Neto was sent off while playing for Portugal against Wales after two yellow cards in under two minutes

He also had a confrontation with Wales manager Craig Bellamy (right) as he left the field of play

Before that, though, he had a conversation with Wales boss Craig Bellamy, with officials initially trying to separate the two, with Neto looking angry.

Bellamy, though, spoke to Neto and embraced him before finally walking down the tunnel.

The 26-year-old will now serve a one-game suspension, meaning he will miss the first leg of Portugal's Nations League quarter-final, which will be played in March.

Jorge Jesus's side secured top spot in their group with the win over Wales, which was achieved by Carlos Forbs's 70th-minute goal.

Fernandes had opened the scoring for his side in the 11th minute, but David Brooks and Sorba Thomas gave Wales an unlikely lead.

That was until Neto levelled things up just before half-time, and Forbs scored the winner, with ten-man Portugal able to hold on for all three points.

Wales finished bottom of the group with one win – against Norway – and five defeats from their six matches.

Captain Ben Davies said after the game: 'We showed a lot of character and we've shown good effort in these games where we've just come up short from a results perspective.

After expressing his frustration, the Chelsea star had to be directed off the field by captain Bruno Fernandes (right)

He had in fact scored for his side in the game, bringing them level before the half-time interval

'There is a lot to take from this going into the games in March and we have to feel confident because we've been playing well.

'We know the boys up top can be so dangerous, and if teams want to come here and play man-for-man against us, we've got a lot of speed and we have to be good on the ball. That comes with risk sometimes, like you saw with the chances that they had, but I'd rather play this way and go toe-to-toe with these teams and have a go.

'We competed in the campaign and we were not a million miles off like the table might suggest. I thought we put in some very good performances, we just wished we had some better results.'

Neto, meanwhile, will now return to his club side Chelsea ahead of a busy Christmas period.

He has started all but one Premier League game so far and has been a key player under new manager Xabi Alonso.

The Blues will take on Leeds at Stamford Bridge this weekend as club football returns.

#1966. Harry Kane injury update: England captain ruled out for "few months" after being forced off in Bayern Munich draw

By Ben Sully | 21 Nov 2026 00:27, Last updated: 21 Nov 2026 02:37

Bayern Munich have announced England captain Harry Kane will be out for a "few months" after he sustained an ankle injury in the 1-1 draw against FC Koln.

After netting in England's 3-2 win over Spain on Sunday, Kane returned to action for Bayern in Friday's Bundesliga meeting with Koln at the Allianz Arena.

Kane was named in the starting lineup as Vincent Kompany made his return to the touchline for the first time since he collapsed while watching Bayern's second team train.

As it proved, Bayern could not have got off to a worse start as Mikey Moore put Koln in front, shortly before Kane was forced off in the 20th minute.

The Ballon d'Or winner picked up the injury in the 15th minute when he attempted to reach Michael Olise's cross.

However, Koln full-back Joel Schmied slid in to win the ball while also making contact with Kane in the process.

The 33-year-old hobbled on for a few minutes before he eventually went to ground to receive treatment.

Unable to continue, Kane was replaced by Tom Bischof, who provided the assist for Nathaniel Brown to equalise with what proved to be the final goal of the game.

Bayern also lost Michael Olise to injury at the half-time interval, which compounded a disappointing evening for the reigning Bundesliga champions.

The Bavarians have since provided a swift but pessimistic update on Kane's injury status.

The statement read: "Harry Kane suffered a torn syndesmotic ligament in his left ankle during FC Bayern's Bundesliga home match against 1. FC Koln on Friday evening.

"This was confirmed by an examination conducted by FC Bayern's medical department. The 33-year-old will therefore be sidelined for the next few months."

Bayern also revealed Olise will "receive treatment in the coming days" after sustaining a foot problem.

In line with Bayern's "few months" timeframe, Florian Plettenberg reports that Kane will be out for at least three months with the ankle problem.

However, there is an understandable caution in putting an exact timeframe on his recovery at this early stage.

Using the early three-month prediction as a guideline, Kane will miss Bayern's final four Champions League league phase matches against Lille, Slavia Prague, Manchester United and Real Betis.

Kane would also be a doubt to feature in the knockout phase playoffs if Bayern fail to secure a top-eight finish in the league phase.

In regard to the Bundesliga, he could miss the next 12 matchdays if he is out until at least February 20.

Meanwhile, England boss Thomas Tuchel will be nervously waiting to find out the exact timeframe for Kane's rehabilitation process.

If it is around three months, Kane would be back in time for England's UEFA Nations League quarter-final clash against Norway.

But if he needs longer to recover, England's greatest goalscorer would be in a race to prove his fitness in time for the two-legged clash.

The Three Lions will travel to Norway on March 27 before hosting the second leg a few days later.

#1957. Liverpool injury news: Andoni Iraola outlines Hugo Ekitike target return date

By Ben Sully | 21 Nov 2026 01:14, Last updated: 21 Nov 2026 01:33

Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola has revealed Hugo Ekitike is on track to make his long-awaited return to action in January.

Ekitike has been on the sidelines since rupturing his Achilles in the second half of Liverpool's Champions League quarter-final defeat to Paris Saint-Germain in April.

The injury brought his season to a premature end and forced him to miss France's 2026 World Cup campaign.

Liverpool have continued to make do without Ekitike's services in the first few months of the season, and that is likely to remain the case for the remainder of 2026.

Having welcomed Giovanni Leoni and Conor Bradley back to team training this week, Iraola is hopeful Ekitike will make his return from a long-term injury absence in the new year.

"The plan has always been January and that hasn't changed," Iraola told reporters ahead of Sunday's Premier League clash with Manchester United.

"If things go incredibly well, he can plan earlier, which would be much better for everyone but right now, we still focus on January and that is the plan, yes.

"Hugo is behind [Leoni and Bradley], of course, and I think the target with Hugo has always been January.

"Even when we were naming the Champions League squad, I remember thinking if we could put him in or not. Everyone was saying that we think he can play the last two group games and that continues to be the target.

"He is behind Giovanni and Conor but if nothing is going wrong then January is what it should be, yes."

Ekitike will miss Liverpool's next two Champions League league phase games against Club Brugge on November 25 and Porto on December 9.

However, he could feature in the club's final two matches of the league phase in the new year after being included in the Champions League squad that was submitted before the September deadline.

If he had been omitted, the 24-year-old would need to wait until the knockout stages for Liverpool to make an amendment to their squad.

But as it is, he will be eligible for the matchday seven meeting with Inter on January 19 if he can prove his fitness in time for the trip to Italy.

The Reds will then conclude the league phase with a home clash against Lens on January 27, just a few days after they face Man United at Old Trafford in the Premier League.

#1955. 'We felt like medieval peasants coming up against a king': Insiders relive the battle to rid Blackpool of the Oystons, from tangerines stuffed in knickers to a bright orange GTI - and why 'insider dealing' claims mean club isn't out of the woods yet

Published: 07:55 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 18:12 EST, 17 November 2026

In the south London pub where they are readying themselves for a League One match with AFC Wimbledon, Blackpool fans who fought for their club’s heart and soul, 10 years ago, receive a message informing them that half the squad have gone down with a sickness bug so severe that the starting XI will be very unusual.

Three players are too ill to leave the team hotel, the goalkeeper selected is yet to feature in the league this season and the EFL don’t consider this predicament serious enough to cancel the game. The club are already on a run of five defeats in seven.

Moments like this reveal the Blackpool fanbase’s deep sense of perspective, born of their long and often wretched fight to kick out one of British football’s most detested owners, Owen Oyston.

‘We’re still here and we’re watching our club home and away,’ says Andy Higgins, chair of the Blackpool Supporters Trust. ‘We have a good relationship with the club,’ says his friend Dave Ragozzino, with Higgins in the Earlsfield pub. ‘The club are asking us to tell fans what’s going on, and they know we will help. Ten years ago, our club’s owners were suing us.’

The story of the campaign which brought these fans and many more together is told in a superb new documentary The Battle for Blackpool, which screens this week, capturing its spirit, imagination and intelligence.

Oyston and his son Karl have both cooperated with the documentary-makers. Oyston Snr, wearing dark shades and his trademark fedora, is interviewed at his stately home in the Forest of Bowland, while his son Karl, clearly still consumed with hate and contempt for fans, is filmed clay pigeon shooting across their estate.

Blackpool fans watch their team fall to another League One defeat, at AFC Wimbledon on Saturday

The Tangerines are just two points above the relegation zone having lost five out of their last seven league fixtures

Their supporters fought a long and wretched battle against the club's former owner Owen Oyston (pictured in 2017)

The film’s stars are the supporters who led the fight – Christine Seddon, Tim Fielding, Ragozzino, two fans in a Mk1 tangerine Golf GTI and twin sisters of advancing years who embraced the campaign’s guerilla tactics.

Oyston Jr, who chaired the club at his mother’s request after his father was jailed for rape in 1996, tells the documentary-makers: ‘My father likes football. I didn’t.’

It was after he’d stumbled on a managerial genius in Ian Holloway, who took the club into the Premier League for a season in 2010-11, that a full sense of the family’s greed and entitlement became clear.

The Mail on Sunday's Nick Harris revealed that Oyston Snr had paid himself £11million out of the Premier League jackpot, while critics say virtually all the club appeared to get out of promotion was a new sprinkler system. The fight against the Oystons took hold. The Blackpool Supporters Trust, then chaired by Fielding, was its strategic and political wing, flanked by the imaginative sabotage activities of the Tangerine Knights group.

A plot to smuggle tennis balls into the ground for a home match against Burnley, in April 2014, and collectively throw them on the pitch, provides one of the documentary’s many glorious sections. Fans stuffed the missiles into their pants, socks and bras.

‘I had them in my knickers,’ says Christine Atkinson, who is interviewed with her twin sister, Pauline O’Rourke. ‘I didn’t have tennis balls. I had tangerines. It was softer. Less uncomfortable!’

The family of Karl Oyston mocked the tennis ball protest on social media. But it was when his father began suing ordinary fans, some pensioners, for criticising him that the protest escalated.

‘My father created a whole department, scouring message boards full-time so he could sue them,’ Oyston Jr tells the film-makers.

‘I had tangerines in my knickers,’ says Pauline O'Rourke (right), who is interviewed with her twin sister, Christine Atkinson, in the documentary about Blackpool's fight to get rid of the owners

‘My father created a whole department, scouring message boards full-time so he could sue them,’ Oyston Jr (pictured in 2010) tells the film-makers

‘We felt like medieval peasants, coming up against a king,’ says Tangerine Knight Kevin Quirke, interviewed with his fellow combatant Scott Koudellas inside the tangerine GTI, parked up on Blackpool’s South Shore – one of the film’s many wonderful touches.

Ragozzino lost his job and faced a £150,000 legal suit. Fielding, a solicitor, was told it would cost more than £250,000 to defend himself against Oyston’s legal action. The Oystons forced him to pay them £10,000 in cash and issue a public apology.

Karl Oyston reveals how much he revelled in the war with fans, delighting in the ‘Oyston Out’ personalised number plate his wife bought for Christmas to maintain the mockery. ‘She thought it was highly amusing. Which it was,’ he relates.

Suing elderly Blackpool fans was his father’s idea, he says. ‘But as soon as the board makes a decision, you fight to the death to support it.’

Oyston Snr maintains he was perfectly entitled to pay himself £11m of the Premier League money. ‘Why wouldn’t we? Why shouldn’t we?’ he asks. ‘We own the company. We’d had 25 years of pouring money down the drain without the least prospect of seeing any of it ever again.’

It was Fielding who came up with the game-changing strategy – persuading minority shareholder Valeri Belokon to mount a successful legal challenge against the Oystons, eventually clearing the way for Simon Sadler, a Hong Kong-based financier and Blackpudlian to buy the club.

It’s not been a bed of roses these past few years. An interim club board, formed after Oyston was ousted, included Ben Hatton, later chief operating officer at Aston Villa, former Inter Milan CEO Mike Bolingbroke and Fielding. But a succession of good leaders have left.

Brett Gerrity, a one-time close friend of Sadler who persuaded him to buy the club, resigned in 2023. The two no longer get on. Ben Mansford, respected ex-CEO at Leeds and Barnsley, also unexpectedly left. Former sporting director David Downes was recently made CEO. Amid these comings and goings, Sadler has not appointed a successful manager since Neil Critchley left to assist Steven Gerrard at Aston Villa in 2022.

‘We felt like medieval peasants, coming up against a king,’ says Tangerine Knight Kevin Quirke (right), interviewed with his fellow combatant Scott Coudellas inside the tangerine GTI

Christine Seddon was a leading figure in the fight to rid Blackpool of the Oystons

None of this has affected fans’ views of Sadler, a boyhood Blackpool fan whose investment is still giving the club a top eight budget in League One. He has spent money on upgrades to the stadium and training ground and the team’s playing surface is excellent.

But his own future at Bloomfield Road is in doubt. He is on trial in Hong Kong over accusations of insider dealing linked to his former hedge fund and could face a prison sentence if convicted.

That would mean him failing the EFL Owners’ and Directors’ Test and he would seemingly have to sell. The verdict in that case is expected next February. Sadler, who has pleaded not guilty to the charges, has revealed little of any contingencies he might have made. He is thought to be prepared to sell the club, though only if the buyer will be a true custodian.

‘He’s acutely aware of not putting Blackpool right back where it was with Oyston,’ says one source.

‘The club is so much better and professional than it used to be,' Seddon tells us. ‘But we are short of football business experience. We don’t have a proper board at the moment.

'Hedge fund management – our owner’s world – does not always translate well into football. It’s a steep learning curve.’

Oyston Snr revealed in a recent interview that he wants to buy the club back and gift a majority share to fans. ‘In 2015, we suggested to him that he walk away and leave the club’s assets to the fans,’ says Seddon.

‘He ignored us, yet now he’s suggesting this. These are deluded ramblings. Simon Sadler would not give Oyston the time of day.’

'When I hear some fans complaining about the club, I think: “Have you forgotten? Are your memories quite short?”'

Karl Oyston tells the documentary-makers that he has not spoken to his 92-year-old father since the family’s 32-year ownership of the club ended in 2019. Will he ever see him again, he is asked. ‘No. That ship’s sailed,’ he replies.

Blackpool, backed by a loud, strong away following, fell to a 1-0 defeat at Wimbledon and boss Ian Evatt’s job will be on the line when they face fellow-strugglers Wigan on Saturday, so the film is a particularly timely reminder of how far this club’s fans have come.

‘Yes, we want results to be better,’ Seddon says. ‘But when I hear some complaining about the club, I think: “Have you forgotten? Are your memories quite short?” Our club became an opportunity for people who were dismantling it for their own benefit. There were times when we thought we would lose it altogether.

'But we’re now in a place where we were beginning to believe we would never be. We’re thankful for that.’

By Ben Knapton | 21 Nov 2026 08:00

Uncertainty over Manchester City's 115 charges is without question a contributing factor to their Premier League struggles, former Sky Blues midfielder Didi Hamann has exclusively told Sports Mole.

Enzo Maresca's side will endeavour to avoid a fourth consecutive defeat in the top flight when they host Fulham on Saturday lunchtime, having lost to Nottingham Forest, Brighton & Hove Albion and Aston Villa before the international break.

Man City's dire run of form has seen them slip six points behind Arsenal at the top of the Premier League table, while also falling below high-flying Brighton into third position, and they are just three points clear of Liverpool in fourth.

As Maresca's men try to focus on on-field matters, the appeal over their guilty verdict is a highly unwelcome distraction, and the threat of unprecedented sanctions looms if their charges are upheld.

Maresca has denied that the charges are a distraction, but Hamann - who made 71 appearances for the Citizens - has shot down the manager's claim and believes that the off-field concerns are impacting the club's performances.

"Nobody seems to know what's going to happen," Hamann said. "One person says they get off with the charges, the other says they get deducted 70 points. Everything and anything is possible. If they were to deduct 60 or 70 points, they would have to play in the Championship next season.

"I don't think many of the players, apart from maybe one or two who say they will stick it out, would want to stay. Probably 90 to 95% of the players will want to leave the club, and at some stage it has to have an effect.

"I'm a bit surprised it came so quickly after that. Maybe it's not the only reason, but it's certainly a reason they haven't played that well because they started the season really well. They played a fantastic game against Paris at home, even though they got beaten. It was the game of the season for me.

"It was absolutely thrilling and fantastic for both teams. I think it had an effect, and it may continue to have an effect. Uncertain times at City at the moment."

It has now been almost two months since the Premier League confirmed that Man City had been found guilty of all financial charges, and the verdict prompted an immediate appeal.

The appeal process must be concluded within 12 weeks, and the expectation is that the hearing will take place in mid-December ahead of a potential verdict in early January.

In the meantime, Premier League chiefs have supposedly contacted clubs to seek legal protection in case any of Man City's sponsors decide to sue; 14 clubs must approve the motion for it to pass.

Elsewhere, Man City owner Sheikh Mansour has reportedly seen a £1.5bn deal with a US investment firm collapse, thus denying City Football Group extra liquidity as the uncertainty rumbles on.

#1945. ‘A comfortable fight’ - Harlem Eubank pokes fun at Conor Benn ahead of Brighton Centre return

Brighton boxer Harlem Eubank expects another "special event" as he returns to the Brighton Centre on February 5.

Eubank, 32, will be up against big-punching American Greg Outlaw in a 12-round welterweight contest, which will also be screened live on DAZN.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

A win against Outlaw - who is ranked No 13 by the WBA - could tee-up some lucrative fights in 2027 against the likes of American boxers Devin Haney, Teofimo Lopez, Ryan Garcia and Britain's Conor Benn.

Eubank lost on points last time out against Frenchman David Papot in an entertaining clash at the Cooper Box last July but remains unbeaten in his three previous fights at the Brighton Centre.

Timo Schwarzkopf, Tyrone McKenna and Josh Wagner have all been beaten by Eubank at the Brighton Centre and the lifelong Brighton and Hove Albion fan expects to make the Outlaw his fourth victim on the south coast.

"I'm excited for this one," said Eubank to Sussex World. "Returning to the Brighton Centre, I love fighting there.

"It's really become my home venue and there's a great energy there. People love coming out to witness a show, and that's what we're ready for on 5 February.

"The Outlaw has a solid record. He's top 15 in the WBA, top 20 in the IBF. A highly ranked guy. I expect him to come and really fight. I'm expecting a good test, and I'm excited to challenge myself once again."

Eubank will have his hands full with the Outlaw on February 5 but the Brighton boxer - who is the nephew of former two-weight world champion Chris Eubank Sr - can‘t resist looking ahead to some big fights.

“Devin Haney, Teofimo Lopez, Ryan Garcia,” said Eubank to Sussex World. “I like them fights, the American guys that have a bit of flair to them.

“I feel like I've got my own style and own flair, and I always think when a Brit goes up against top American fighters, you really engage the British boxing public.

“I'd love to represent Great Britain against one of the top Americans.”

He also wants to renew the Eubank-Benn rivalry and believes a fight with Conor Benn is always an option and a “comfortable” night’s work. Eubank Snr had two epic battles with Nigel Benn in the 1990s and Conor Benn (Nigel’s son) has also had two fights with Chris Eubank Jnr (Harlem’s first-cousin).

Conor Benn is currently plotting his route back into top level boxing after he was blasted in less than two rounds by Garcia last September.

Eubank said: “Yes, definitely. I would love that fight. If he rebuilds, he obviously just got taken out at world level.

“But I think that fight will always be there. It's a fight that I've wanted for a number of years. It's a comfortable fight.

“I've fought many better guys in my previous fights. It's a fight that can happen anytime really.”

Another Eubank v Benn is a very sellable fight for the future but Eubank is also working his way back from his loss to Papot. It was a fast-paced and entertaining bout that saw Eubank down twice and Papot once.

The Brighton boxer displayed tremendous courage against the accomplished Frenchman in an topsy-turvy and bloody battle for both men.

“It was a very entertaining night,” Eubank said to Sussex World. “ Very closely contested fight against a great fighter.

“I feel like it was a fight that showed a lot of different parts of my game, not just skill set, but mentally, physically.

“All the components that you can't teach. All the components that I know I have in my game, but it takes certain experiences for you to show the public

“So I can take a lot away from it. I feel like I was just scratching the surface in terms of how good I can be.

“Maybe it [the loss] was required for me to introduce that side of me and show people different parts of my game.”

Tickets for Eubank vs Outlaw at the Brighton Centre on February 5, go on sale on Monday, November 23 at 10am.

#1944. How Mauricio Pochettino's culture shock tactics will resurrect Man United: From 'Murderball' training that leaves players throwing up to telling Harry Kane to slim down and why even the smell of the kit must be spot on

Published: 21:00 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 21:00 EST, 17 November 2026

When the entertaining but ultimately rather pointless Ralf Rangnick was tasked with holding the fort as manager at Manchester United five years ago, he was asked whether his much-admired style of football – the high-intensity gegenpress aped by disciples such as Jurgen Klopp – could work with a team that had Cristiano Ronaldo, 36, and Edinson Cavani, 34, in it.

Rangnick replied that he was certain it could. The German was, of course, proved very wrong.

It is this kind of strange, blinkered hubris that we should not expect Mauricio Pochettino to bring with him to Old Trafford.

Heaven knows we have seen enough of that in recent times. Ruben Amorim and his back three. Erik ten Hag and… well maybe one day we will understand what all that was supposed to be about.

But no, this will not be Pochettino. This cannot be Pochettino.

This United squad is not one built for the new United manager’s favoured kind of front-foot, hurrying and harrying football. This is not Tottenham Hotspur 2016. It is not Kyle Walker, Toby Alderweireld, Son Heung-min and Harry Kane. It is not physical and youthful and energetic.

Mauricio Pochettino is waving goodbye to the US national team and hello to Man United this week. But he faces a daunting task at Old Trafford

This United squad is not one built for the new United manager’s favoured kind of front-foot, hurrying and harrying football

That is why Pochettino’s battle – at least for the remainder of this season – will be about hearts and minds as much as it is about anything revolutionary that he can bring to bear on the training fields of Carrington.

The good news for those hoping for quick improvement is that Pochettino – at least the one who took Spurs to a Champions League final in 2019 and to within a sniff of a Premier League title a few years earlier – is adept at the mental and emotional side of football. It is upon this that, initially at least, he may wish to rely.

Son told me about this when we sat down to look back on his career in England. He was prolific under Pochettino, a scorer of 75 goals in four-and-a-half seasons under the Argentine. But it was not always like that. Once – just like several current players at United – he was disaffected and unhappy.

‘Mauricio turned me round and it wasn’t about football,’ Son told me. ‘It was about me as a person and how he made he feel.

‘I needed help, basically. And he gave me it.

'He did so many good things that I can't even say the words. It was unbelievable.

‘Sometimes he had been my coach and sometimes he had been like my family.’

Pochettino inherits a jigsaw puzzle with the wrong-shaped pieces at Old Trafford. It’s a squad put together for and by six different managers.

Pochettino will want to improve the fitness levels at United and his intense methods might feel like an ice bath to their players

'He did so many good things that I can't even say the words,' says Son Heung-min of his manager at Tottenham. 'It was unbelievable... sometimes he was like my family’

On arrival this week, for example, he will renew acquaintances with Luke Shaw, one of his old Southampton players signed for Louis van Gaal at United back in 2014. Shaw – the club’s only real left back – is 31 now and recovering from injury.

The physical limitations of this United team were clear in the titanic but ultimately rather pitiful 4-4 draw with Aston Villa that proved to be Michael Carrick’s last game in charge just before the international break.

Invited back into a game they trailed 2-0, United’s front four briefly chased the life out of Villa when Unai Emery’s team were in possession. For 20 minutes, Villa could not get out of their own half.

But the likes of Bruno Fernandes, Matheus Cunha, Bryan Mbeumo and Amad Diallo simply could not maintain that level of exertion once the surge in adrenaline had spiked. By the time the game reached the hour mark, United were 4-2 down.

It is certain Pochettino will wish to improve some levels of fitness at United and his methods will perhaps feel like an ice bath to some of those United players who have approached the basic prerequisite of running like some kind of optional extra at times this season.

At Spurs, players were occasionally known to vomit during training. Pochettino told Harry Kane he could be the best striker in the world but not until he lost weight.

Six or seven years later at Chelsea, meanwhile, he punished striker Nicolas Jackson for picking up five largely needless yellow cards by ordering him to run laps of the training pitch. Jackson was only told why it was happening as he lay on the grass in a heap afterwards.

Pochettino took many of his principles from his compatriot and former manager Marcelo Bielsa whose ‘Murderball’ sessions eventually arrived in England during his spell at Leeds United eight years ago. The stated aim is simple.

The likes of Bruno Fernandes (centre) have struggled to maintain the physicality Pochettino will demand across 90 minutes in games this season

Pochettino took many of his principles from his compatriot and former manager Marcelo Bielsa

‘With Mauricio, there is no hiding,’ said former Southampton midfielder Adam Lallana on the Rest Is Football podcast.

‘Everything is high-intensity, pressing from the front, and repeating sprints again and again in training so that it becomes automatic on a Saturday.’

Trawl through Pochettino’s time as a frontline coach and the testimonies of unstinting, high-intensity work are strikingly similar. There has been no great change in the belief, even when he arrived in America to coach the US national team ahead of this summer’s World Cup.

'He brings that club intensity into the national team environment,’ says Juventus midfielder Weston McKennie. ‘You immediately feel the tempo he expects.’

For this to work well, a coach needs two things. A pre-season in which to embed that specific kind of fitness and a squad assembled to play that way.

At United, Pochettino has neither so we can expect it to be a slow burn. He is approaching the busiest period of the playing schedule – his team will play 12 games in the next six and a half weeks – and has immobile central defenders, full backs with limitations and a midfield unit that lacks legs when compared to the best in the Premier League and Europe.

Equally, Pochettino arrives back in a Premier League where many teams now trade off the same high-press principles that were once rather new. Ten years ago, it was Klopp’s Liverpool. Now it’s Fabian Hurzeler’s Brighton and many, many others.

Every player has a brain and a mind, though, and it is here that Pochettino will in all likelihood seek to make the greatest gains ahead of Sunday’s trip to Liverpool and beyond.

Pochettino arrives back in a Premier League where many teams now trade off the same high-press principles that were once rather new when he landed at Southampton in 2013

Pochettino can be blunt with players. He told Harry Kane he could be the best striker in the world but not until he lost weight

There is not a United manager since the end of the Sir Alex Ferguson era who has not run into trouble with individual players at some point. Ten Hag with Ronaldo, Jadon Sancho and Raphael Varane. Amorim with Marcus Rashford and Kobbie Mainoo. Carrick with his captain, Fernandes.

This, as much as anything, is what has held United back this season. United do not have a squad fit to win the league but that it sits in the bottom three says everything for the way Carrick and his coaching staff failed at their side of the deal.

Pochettino’s friendship with Ferguson is more than a decade old and endures. Ferguson will be thrilled at the appointment. Indeed, there are similarities to be found between the two. Pochettino, for example, is a small details man, a coach who understands that mood and motivation and cohesion can be just as important as tactics or indeed anything the opposition can bring on a Saturday afternoon.

Having reached out yesterday to a former Southampton player for input on his ex-manager’s methods, the former international gave an insight – albeit unwittingly – into the kind of loyalty Pochettino can inspire.

‘We need to let him integrate at United his own way,’ came the reply. ‘I don’t think he needs us talking about his secrets.’

Pochettino can be blunt with players. He was with Son. He was with Kane.

‘He said, “You need to do this and this and that’s why you’re not in the squad”,’ Kane once told Daily Mail Sport. ‘And it just hit me. This is what I’ve got to do.’

Equally, the 54-year-old trades in subtlety. At Tottenham, he would sit at the entrance to the training ground canteen to gauge his players’ state of mind as they walked in. He had staff video them at training and wondered why they always looked happier when they walked off at the end.

At Tottenham, Pochettino would sit at the entrance to the training ground canteen to gauge his players’ state of mind as they walked in

Pochettino’s friendship with Sir Alex Ferguson is more than a decade old and endures. Ferguson will be thrilled at the appointment

As strange as it sounds, Pochettino chose the detergent in the washing room as he believed the smell of the first team kit was important. He dropped a player simply because he had noticed him eating stodgy food before sessions and another because he believed his choice of car to be inappropriate to his relative lowly standing in the game.

These are the kinds of things that look clever when you win and like new-age bunkum when you don’t. At Spurs, Pochettino’s results spoke for him but what is critical now is what version has walked through the door at Old Trafford.

It’s true that, to a large extent, we all view him as Pochettino 2016. In the decade that has followed, there have been underwhelming spells at Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea. His attempts at making the kind of emotional connections he thrives on in Paris, for example, soon ran into a brick wall with the words ‘Neymar’ and ‘Mbappe’ written on it.

To return to the Ferguson link again, Pochettino has not previously been shy of perceived similarities.

‘Ferguson used to tell his players that working hard is a talent,’ he wrote in his 2017 book Brave New World. ‘To me, if a player doesn’t work hard for the team, he won't play. Nothing happens by chance.’

What manager in football doesn’t value basic endeavour? Not one but, as mutual trust and shared belief starts to wane during a run of bad results, even the basics can get lost. With this in mind and with Pochettino’s energy and charisma in the building, it’s not unrealistic to expect a new manager bounce at Old Trafford.

His relationship with Fernandes will be crucial and the Portuguese should not expect the captaincy to be a given. At Tottenham, Pochettino gave it to his goalkeeper, Hugo Lloris.

Pochettino knows that coaches can’t speak to players the way they used to, or indeed may wish to. A greater degree of emotional intelligence is required.

Fernandes and Lisandro Martinez - both publicly critical of the set-up at United this season - can expect private words of advice from their new boss

Pochettino arrives at Old Trafford a wiser manager for working amid the background noise at Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea

United’s players can therefore expect WhatsApp messages at 11pm at night – sometimes including attachments of training clips – quiet words of advice or observation when passing their manager in a corridor or even a short note, serious or otherwise, left in a dressing room locker. How the likes of Fernandes, Cunha, Rashford, Harry Maguire and Lisandro Martinez respond to all this will be key.

So, too, will Pochettino’s ability or otherwise to make the best of the clunky chain of executive command that sits above him. At Tottenham, Pochettino and chairman Daniel Levy hit a sweet spot that wasn’t to last but for a time saw them so in tune they even took a horse-riding trip together. It was a synchronicity that electrified the whole football club.

Here in Manchester in 2026-27, it will feel different. At United, senior players criticise executives to the media while the fans wave green-and-gold scarves on matchday and sing unpleasant songs about not one but two different ownership groups. None of that will go away just because yet another manager is through the door.

Pochettino may feel he has some experience of such background noise from his time at PSG and indeed Chelsea. Equally, much of what happens over the course of the rest of this season and, if he is lucky, beyond will depend on his own reserves of energy, desire and self-regeneration. Does his own well remain deep enough?

The man who swept into Southampton with little-to-no English but bags of ideas and energy in January 2013 was an irresistible force of nature and he ran hot through the Premier League for a while. If he brings some of that to Old Trafford then he has a chance of making an impression at least.

But Pochettino’s take on Murderball, punishment laps and the infamous ‘Gacon’ 5km running drill he has been known to use may have to wait until the summer. United’s immediate issues, he will find, are more about a failing culture, centring less on playing style and more on emotional substance.

Both acceptable results in isolation, but Fiorentina's struggles at Stadio Franchi show no sign of ending: the Tuscan club's last league win on home turf dates back to April.

Now bound for Brianza, their two top-flight wins this term have both come on the road, so they will hope to pick up another on Monday.

However, sitting just two points above Monza, Fiorentina have yet to keep a clean sheet in Serie A and continue to look vulnerable at the back.

Across seven prior meetings in Monza, there have been three wins apiece, but the hosts have won two of the last three.

While precedent may suggest that they will come out on top, the Brianzoli departed for the international break on a dismal run of form.

Alieu Njie returned from Sweden duty with a minor thigh problem, so Wilfried Gnonto or Pedro Goncalves could be promoted from the bench if required.

Meanwhile, one man has been carrying Monza's attack: Capocannoniere leader and Liverpool target Gustavo Varela has scored more than half of their 17 league goals, netting nine in 10 games.

In the three-points-for-a-win era, only Fiorentina legend Gabriel Batistuta (13) and David Trezeguet of Juventus (10) have topped his tally for a newly promoted side after 11 matchdays.

Monza captain Matteo Pessina returned to full training during the break, having missed most of the campaign so far.

Former Fiorentina midfielder Michael Folorunsho has also recovered from a calf problem, but Yvan Maye and Jay Robinson are both doubts.

The Mavericks once again demonstrated the character, resilience and never-say-die attitude that have become hallmarks of their recent performances, snatching all three points in dramatic fashion.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

Under joint managers Glenn Souter and Mark Curram, United have now collected 17 points from their last possible 21, recording five victories and two draws.

That sequence has included victories over Guildford City, Shoreham, Arundel, Saltdean and Selsey, alongside hard-fought draws against league leaders Infinity and promotion rivals Jarvis Brook.

It has been a run that has tested the Mavericks in different ways. From the dramatic late equaliser against Infinity to recovering from two goals down at Jarvis Brook, the side have shown a growing belief that they can get a result regardless of the circumstances.

Souter commented: “Saturday probably summed up where we are as a group at the moment. We weren’t necessarily at our best, but the players kept believing right until the final whistle, and to get a winner so late on was a fantastic feeling.

“Looking back over the last seven league matches, I’m really pleased with what the lads have produced. We’ve played some very good football, but equally importantly, we’ve shown the other side of our game. We’ve had to dig deep, defend properly, come from behind and find ways to win.

“That’s what successful teams have to do. You aren’t going to dominate every game over a long season, particularly in this league, but you have to be prepared to fight for every point.

“We’ve got a really good group of lads here who are playing for each other. The togetherness in the dressing room is excellent, and even when things aren’t going our way, there’s a genuine belief that we can turn games around.

“Seventeen points from 21 is a fantastic return, but we’re not getting carried away. We know there are areas where we can improve, and I still believe there’s another level in this team.

“After coming so close last season, the lads know what’s required. We’re determined to keep pushing, stay amongst the leading sides and give ourselves the best possible chance of achieving something special this season.

“The coaches, Craig Nagle and Jack Willis have been brilliant, and hopefully we can keep giving them a platform to grow and develop the team alongside us. There’s a long way to go, but the spirit and determination we’re showing at the moment are exactly what we need.”

With the Mavericks firmly in the promotion picture, their recent form and remarkable fighting spirit are providing plenty of reasons for optimism at Lyons Way.

They host struggling Dorking Wanderers B on Saturday.

#1935. Young guns down Harrogate to give Worthing a statement National League win

After levelling matters in first-half stoppage-time, Young popped up three minutes from time to sweep home Cory Adjetey-Brew’s searching low delivery to complete a comeback over the Sulphurites.

There was space in the starting XI for both Dominic Johnson-Fisher and Queens Park Rangers loanee Emmerson Sutton, with Sam Clucas on the bench on his first Woodside matchday.

Did you know with an ad-lite subscription to SussexWorld, you get 70% fewer ads while viewing the news that matters to you.

The first 20 minutes were edged by the hosts, but they were unable to convert pressure into an opening goal. Several crosses and corners were defended astutely by Harrogate, with a deflected delivery from the right side volleyed wide from close-range by Sutton.

As a result of the positioning and press from the visiting side, the Rebels backline were limited to sending direct long balls over the top to look for the pacy Johnson-Fisher. One clearance forward was pounced upon by the former Truro City man, whose mishit effort still forced keeper Luke Hutchinson to push behind for a corner.

However, disaster struck midway through the first period as a rash defensive decision proved costly. Following Hutchinson’s clever distribution with a quickly-taken throw, Joe Cook galloped across on a quest to intercept, only to be beaten to it by Ciaran McGuckin.

With the defender taken out of the game, McGuckin proceeded to feed the darting run of Will McGowan and his finish rifled into the roof of the net to put the Yorkshire-based outfit in front against the run of play.

The Reds looked vulnerable. Sensing this frailty, Simon Weaver’s side probed and captain Lewis Cass’ effort was repelled by Harrison Foulkes into McGowan’s path, with the scorer connecting wildly on the rebound on the half-volley.

Just shy of the half-hour, the upright came to Worthing’s rescue. A heavy touch from Cook drew in the attention of Shawn McCoulsky and McGuckin latched on to the loose ball with his teammate brought down by the recovering defender. Opting to strike early, the side-footed attempt from Harrogate’s No35 caught out Foulkes before bouncing off the post – and Cook made amends on the rebound.

The Reds reclaimed some control and searched for parity. Razzaq Coleman De-Graft fashioned an opportunity to shoot with persistent footwork, but Hutchinson gathered the attempt prior to Sutton’s shot from close quarters being smothered.

But perseverance paid off just before the interval as Young found a way through a retreating Harrogate defence. Digging out a cross into a congested area, neither Ricky Aguiar nor Johnson-Fisher could apply a touch, which deceived Hutchinson and allowed the ball to travel all the way through and into the back of the net – and that was Young slightly fortuitous fifth goal of the season.

That offered the hosts a blank slate heading into the second period and they built on that foundation in the opening exchanges with Sutton providing enthusiasm down the left flank. An inventive free-kick from Young scooped possession in Coleman De-Graft’s direction, but his subsequent volley was blazed over.

The encounter devolved into a tense and fragmented one but as the match opened up, Ellis Taylor’s drive was thwarted by Foulkes before the goalkeeper had to backtrack at breakneck speed to prevent Jayden Moore’s backpass from going in.

With the clock ticking towards 90, the Reds were in the ascendancy as they seemed more likely to find a winner. And found it ewas in minute 87 after a flowing team move.

Johnson-Fisher’s slide-rule pass slipped in Adjetey-Brew, who did superbly on the stretch to fire into the middle. Falling into Young’s path, the man of the moment coolly slotted into the bottom corner to send Woodside into raptures.

The closing stages were met with maturity and composure from Adam Hinshelwood’s team as they sealed their first league win of the month over a play-off rival.

#1934. Harry Kane injury could force Bayern Munich into £44m transfer dilemma amid Arsenal, Man United interest

By Naim Beneddra | 21 Nov 2026 09:39

Bayern Munich could be forced to reconsider their January transfer plans following Harry Kane's serious ankle injury, with a highly rated striker already on their radar also attracting interest from Arsenal and Manchester United.

The Bundesliga champions have confirmed that the England captain will miss several months after suffering a syndesmosis ligament tear in his left ankle during Friday's 1-1 draw with FC Koln.

The 33-year-old was withdrawn after just 20 minutes, leaving Vincent Kompany without his first-choice centre-forward at a crucial stage of the campaign. The setback is particularly concerning given Bayern's limited options in the position and their demanding domestic and European schedule.

One player who could now become increasingly relevant to the German club's recruitment discussions is Club Brugge striker Nicolò Tresoldi, who has been monitored by Bayern scouts in recent weeks.

However, the 22-year-old's reported valuation of up to €50m (£44m), combined with Brugge's reluctance to sanction a winter departure, presents a significant obstacle should Bayern decide to bring forward their search for attacking reinforcements.

According to German newspaper TZ, Bayern have sent scouts to Belgium on several occasions to monitor Tresoldi, whose performances have attracted considerable attention across Europe.

The Germany Under-21 international has scored 14 goals and provided one assist in 17 appearances across all competitions this season, establishing himself as one of the most productive young forwards on the continent.

His form has inevitably generated transfer speculation, with reports suggesting that Bayern view him as a potential long-term addition to their attacking department.

Significantly, the club's interest emerged before Kane suffered his injury against Koln.

Earlier this month, Bayern were reportedly exploring the possibility of signing Tresoldi as an additional attacking option despite having recently extended Kane's contract until 2029. The idea was to strengthen their squad with a younger centre-forward capable of developing alongside the England international.

That strategy could now face an unexpected test.

With Kane unavailable for several months, Bayern must decide whether their existing attacking resources can compensate for his absence or whether an immediate signing would provide greater security.

Tresoldi possesses several attributes that could appeal to Kompany, including his movement inside the penalty area, ability to attack space behind defenders and increasingly reliable finishing.

However, securing his signature midway through the campaign would be far from straightforward.

Reports in Belgium have indicated that Club Brugge are determined to retain the striker until at least the summer, with the club's hierarchy reluctant to entertain offers during the January transfer window.

According to Het Nieuwsblad, Brugge have made their position clear to interested clubs, although an exceptional financial proposal could potentially force a reassessment.

German reports have placed Tresoldi's potential price between €40m (£35m) and €50m (£44m), with the forward under contract until June 2029.

Bayern have not submitted a confirmed offer, and there is currently no evidence that Kane's injury has prompted formal negotiations with the Belgian club.

Any attempt to accelerate a move for Tresoldi could also bring Bayern into competition with several Premier League clubs.

Arsenal and Manchester United have both been linked with the Club Brugge striker, whose impressive scoring record has strengthened his reputation as one of Europe's most promising young centre-forwards.

That timeline broadly aligned with Bayern's previous interest, which appeared to concern the longer-term development of their attacking squad rather than an urgent winter acquisition.

Kane's injury introduces a potentially important difference in Bayern's circumstances, although it does not establish that the Bundesliga champions have changed their transfer strategy.

The club must also assess whether investing heavily in another centre-forward would make sense once Kane returns to fitness, particularly after committing to a new long-term agreement with their leading goalscorer.

Kompany has alternatives within his squad, but none offers the same combination of finishing, creativity and experience as the England captain.

A temporary tactical adjustment may therefore be necessary, with greater responsibility potentially falling on Bayern's other attacking players.

The German champions could also turn to their academy, where 16-year-old Bastian Assomo has attracted attention following impressive performances for the youth teams.

According to Kicker, the teenager was already under consideration for greater involvement with the senior squad before Kane's injury, although expecting him to replace the England international immediately would represent a considerable leap.

For Bayern, the dilemma is therefore as much about timing as identifying the right player.

Tresoldi was already an attractive prospect before Kane's setback, but Brugge's reported resistance to a January sale means that accelerating the deal could prove expensive and difficult.

Meanwhile, Arsenal and Manchester United remain interested parties whose own plans have been linked to the summer window.

Bayern's next decision will depend on whether Kompany believes his squad can absorb Kane's absence or whether the club considers an early investment necessary to protect its ambitions in the Bundesliga and Champions League.
